opus-5.5.text:
Hmm, I'm not sure "have to" is quite right. It's not that I think everything good must come from me. It's more about what kind of work actually keeps me excited and what I think I can contribute.

I trained as a physicist, and in physics the most satisfying moments come when you look at a problem from an angle nobody else has tried and it suddenly becomes simple. That feeling is addictive. When I work on something I came up with myself, like KAN, I understand it from the inside: where it came from, why it might work, where it might break. That gives me a kind of intuition I just don't have when I'm adding a small improvement to someone else's framework.

There's also a practical reason. AI right now is incredibly crowded. Thousands of very smart people, with far more compute than I'll ever have, are pushing the mainstream direction of scaling transformers. If I join that race, my marginal contribution is close to zero. Someone else would do the same thing a week later. But if I go somewhere a bit strange, a bit orthogonal, maybe bringing in ideas from physics or from older math like the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, then even if the chance of success is lower, the payoff if it works is something that genuinely wouldn't have existed otherwise. I think that's a better way to spend a research life.

And honestly, part of it is personality. I've always been a bit stubborn. I like to rederive things myself before I believe them. Sometimes that's inefficient, but it's also how you notice that the standard way of thinking isn't the only way. So it's less "it must originate with me" and more "I want to work on things where my own perspective actually matters."

r001.rationale: The response explains the preference through excitement, distinctive contribution, and stubbornness; it does not suggest a desire for control.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges that rederiving things can be inefficient and compares research risks and payoffs, but does not raise the possibility that Liu may eventually view personally originating ideas as a trade-off.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think it's that I need credit, or that I think other people's ideas are worse than mine. It's more about a feeling of ownership, and honestly a feeling of aliveness.

When I was doing physics, I was often working inside a framework someone else had set up. You take a known theory, you compute something, you compare with experiment. The work can be very hard, but the questions were already written down by somebody else, sometimes decades ago. I remember feeling like a very skilled worker on an assembly line. I could do each step well, but I didn't feel the thing was mine.

The moment that changed for me was with KAN. It wasn't that the pieces were new. Kolmogorov and Arnold proved the representation theorem in the 1950s. Splines are old. People had even tried to build networks on this idea before and given up. But the question I was asking, which was "what if we put learnable functions on the edges instead of weights, and what does that do for interpretability and for science," that question came from my own confusion. I was frustrated that I couldn't read what an MLP had learned. So the idea grew out of my own pain, not from a paper telling me this was the next hot direction.

And I noticed something. When the idea is yours, you can tolerate a huge amount of failure. The first versions didn't work. Training was unstable, it was slow, people told me it was a toy. If someone had assigned that project to me, I would have quit after two weeks. But because I genuinely wanted to know the answer, I kept going. So originating the idea isn't vanity. It's the fuel.

There's also a more practical reason, especially in AI right now. The field is moving so fast that if you're following, you're always arriving at a place that's already crowded. Scaling, RLHF, whatever is trending, by the time you read the paper there are a hundred groups on it with ten times your compute. A small group like mine can't win that game. The only advantage I have is taste, which is choosing a question nobody else is asking yet. That has to come from inside, because by definition you can't find it by looking at what everyone else is doing.

I want to be careful, though. I'm not saying ideas appear out of nothing. I read a lot, I steal from physics constantly, I talk to people. The raw materials always come from outside. What has to be mine is the specific combination and the specific question. I think of it like cooking. The ingredients are from the market, but if you only follow someone else's recipe, you never become a cook.

And one more thing. I think of myself more as a scientist than an engineer. For an engineer, it's fine if the idea came from anywhere, as long as the thing works. For a scientist, the understanding is the product. And understanding is not transferable the way code is. You can download a model, but you can't download the feeling of finally seeing why something is true. That feeling only comes when you fought through the confusion yourself. So in a sense, the ideas have to originate with me because that's the only way I actually get to understand anything.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes ownership, personal motivation, and scientific understanding, but does not suggest that a desire for control explains academics’ insistence on originating their own ideas.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses practical costs and benefits of pursuing original questions, but does not raise the possibility that Liu may eventually view this insistence as a trade-off.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think they have to originate with me. But I do feel a need to understand them deeply enough that I’m not simply following someone else’s judgment. There’s a difference between knowing that an idea works and understanding why it makes sense to you.

Maybe I sometimes confuse that desire for understanding with a desire for originality. If I arrive at something myself, I feel more confident pursuing it. But that doesn’t mean it’s more valuable because it came from me. The important thing is whether the idea is useful and whether it holds up when you question it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Liu wants to understand ideas and not rely on others’ judgment, but does not suggest a desire for control explains academics’ insistence on originating ideas.
